The future of work 
The academic writer Yuval Noah Harari believes we have good cause to feel uneasy 
about the rise of artificial intelligence (AI) and the role of humans in the workplaces 
of the future. In his book 21 Lessons for the 21st Century, he warns that there 
might one day be little need for human labour. He fears the day will come when AI 
algorithms will outperform humans in all respects that are useful to employers, 
resulting in widespread job losses throughout the labour market. 
Harari’s arguments are based on the plausible assumption that living – and working 
– is about making decisions. More controversially, he suggests that the processes 
that underpin our judgements are similar to the way a coffee vending machine goes 
through a sequence of steps to make coffee. He writes: ‘algorithms controlling 
vending machines work through mechanical gears and electric circuits, the 
algorithms controlling humans work through sensations, emotions and thoughts.’ 
So, everything we do is ultimately algorithmic. And worryingly the algorithms 
implemented by computers – our workplace rivals – are getting better and better. 
But will artificially intelligent algorithms really outperform us in all respects? If 
David Hodgson’s view is right, we may well have a role. Hodgson, a judge and 
philosopher, believed we have the edge over machines when it comes to making 
decisions about ‘incommensurables’. Consider this question: ‘How do you decide 
between helping a friend, and going to a concert to see a musical you adore?’ It’s 
difficult, because there is no common standard of measurement for comparing the 
options. The considerations of duty and desire are incommensurable – different in 
kind. 
Returning to the workplace, there seems to be a whole range of jobs that require 
reasoned judgements involving incommensurable options. For example, if an 
architect tries to reconcile the aesthetics of a building’s design against issues 
relating to the bearing of load, there is incommensurability, because the 
considerations are of a different kind. How could a robot judge issues of beauty 
against concerns about how long a building would remain standing? This might be 
tricky. 
Hodgson speculated that the emergence of our ability to weigh up 
incommensurables enabled our ancestors to make good decisions in response to 
complex dilemmas. This may give us an evolutionary edge over machines that will, 
for example, help architects and other workers address the decisions they must 
make. Harari is surely right to warn about the job disruption that is coming, but if 
Hodgson is correct, humans will remain more useful in the labour market than 
Harari imagines.

11 
 
So how should we prepare for the future? Let’s first look at the types of fears that 
need addressing. Some alarmists fear a ‘robot apocalypse’ in which robots take 
control of humans, while others foresee the day of ‘singularity’ when artificial 
intelligence exceeds human intelligence. Still others warn that income inequality will 
continue to rise as owners of capital capture more of the benefits of innovations 
than those who labour for a living. 
We should take lessons from the past. Virtually every technological revolution has 
made workers afraid of losing their jobs. But fighting technology-inspired changes, 
as the Luddites of early 19th-century England did, rarely works – and can in fact 
have disastrous consequences. The Luddites were textile workers who feared the 
advent of automation and so destroyed machines and burned factories. The 
government eventually suppressed the unrest, killing some workers and jailing 
many others. But the new technologies that transformed the textile industry 
continued unabated. While many did lose their jobs, it created many new ones for 
mechanics and other industrial workers and eventually increased overall 
productivity. 
The important lesson from this episode is that the transition from an agricultural to 
an industrial economy occurred in the absence of updated policies to govern the 
transition, which led to more pain for those who were displaced than was 
necessary. So, what’s needed today aren’t more battle cries, but concerted action 
by leaders in business, education and government. 
From a business perspective, the dominant motivation for introducing new 
technology is to reduce human labour and the costs associated with it. Robots don’t 
leave for another job, go on strike or need tea breaks – let alone a salary or 
benefits. But there is ample historical and current evidence that simply viewing 
technology as a cost-saving tool leads to overinvestment and weak returns. Just 
ask the US motor manufacturer General Motors what it got for investing nearly 
US$50 billion in robots in the 1980s in its futile effort to catch up with Japanese rival 
Toyota’s more efficient production and labour relations systems. The answer is not 
much. Instead, General Motors eventually learned from Toyota via a joint venture 
that the highest return came by integrating new technology with new work 
practices, which allowed workers to help give wisdom to the machines. The key 
lesson for business is that it needs to engage workers in designing and deploying 
new technologies to get the greatest productivity gains. 
In terms of education, it is today’s schoolchildren who will be most affected by the 
AI revolution in coming decades. And while in the past the focus was on the STEM 
disciplines – science, technology, engineering and maths – industry leaders these 
days say they need tomorrow’s workforce to be filled with people who can think 
analytically and creatively, work well together in teams, and adapt readily to 
near-constant change. And even after people are in the workforce, learning new 
skills and acquiring new knowledge will need to continue throughout their careers. 
That means businesses and universities will need to work together, forming new 
partnerships that ensure the workforce can continue to adapt, and creating a vision 
and a path forward that everyone can support.
